title: De drei Vügelkens
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 96. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form. The glosses in round brackets inside the text — wünt (gewohnt), de Möhme (Mutter) — are the Grimms’ own and belong to the 1857 text.
about: KHM 96, told entirely in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the dialect of the north, so nearly every word differs from the High German used elsewhere in the collection. Three cowherd girls call out which of a passing king and his ministers they mean to marry, and get their wish; but when the queen bears children marked with a bright red star, her two jealous sisters throw each newborn into the river and tell the king each time that she has borne an animal instead. A bird’s song follows every drowning, a fisherman quietly saves all three children, and years later the grown son and daughter must pass a black dog, a dropped rod, and a well of water to free their imprisoned mother and undo what was done to her — all narrated in the dialect the Grimms recorded it in, with their own glosses in round brackets here and there.

sentences.t: Et is wul dusent un meere Jaare hen, da wören hier im Lanne luter kleine Künige, da hed auck einer up den Keuterberge wünt (gewohnt), de gink san geren up de Jagd.
sentences.l: It is fully a thousand years and more ago; there were here in the land nothing but little kings, and one of them too has dwelt (gewohnt) upon the Keuterberg, who went so gladly to the hunt.
sentences.i: It is a thousand years and more ago now, and there were nothing but little kings here in the land; one of them lived on the Keuterberg, and he went to the hunt very gladly.
sentences.n: This tale is told from beginning to end in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the old speech of the north, and not in the High German of most of the collection, so nearly every word looks a little foreign. Some of the swaps you meet at once: Et = es, is = ist, un = und, dat = das, de = der/die, wören = waren, hed = hat, auck = auch, up = auf, Künige = Könige. The round bracket in “wünt (gewohnt)” is the Grimms’ own: they gloss the Low German word with its High German equivalent for readers outside the dialect area, and the literal line keeps their bracket where it stands. meere here is mehr, more, and has nothing to do with das Meer, the sea. san is an intensifier with geren (gern), “so gladly,” though the form itself is not certainly explained. hen is hin in its old temporal sense, gone by: “dusent un meere Jaare hen” is a thousand years and more gone.

sentences.t: Ase nu mal mit sinen Jägern vom Schlotte herruttrok, höen (hüteten) unner den Berge drei Mäkens ire Köge (Kühe), un wie sei den Künig mit den vielen Lüen (Leuten) seien, so reip de ölleste den annern beden Mäkens to, un weis up den Künig, „helo! helo! wenn ik den nig kriege, so will ik keinen.“
sentences.l: When [he] now once rode out from the castle with his huntsmen, three girls were tending (hüteten) their cows (Kühe) below the hill, and when they saw the king with the many people (Leuten), the eldest called across to the other two girls, and pointed at the king, “helo! helo! if I do not get that one, then I will have none.”
sentences.i: Now when he rode out one day from the castle with his huntsmen, three girls were minding their cows below the hill; and when they saw the king with all his people, the eldest called across to the other two and pointed at the king: “Helo! Helo! If I do not get that one, then I will have none at all.”
sentences.n: Three of the Grimms’ own glosses stand in this one sentence — höen (hüteten), Köge (Kühe), Lüen (Leuten) — and the literal keeps all three. Ase = als, when; herruttrok = herauszog, rode out; sei here is se, sie, they, and seien is not a form of sein but sahen, they saw; weis = wies, the past of weisen, to point; beden = beiden, the two; nig = nicht; reip = rief. helo is a call across a distance, our “hallo.” The German leaves the subject out — “Ase nu mal … herruttrok” — so the English supplies [he]; that bracket is ours, not the Grimms’. mal here is the adverb, einmal, once, and not das Mal, a time.

sentences.t: Da antworde de zweide up de annere Side vom Berge, un weis up den, de dem Künige rechter Hand gink, „helo! helo! wenn ik den nig kriege, so will ik keinen.“
sentences.l: Then the second answered, on the other side of the hill, and pointed at the one who went at the king’s right hand, “helo! helo! if I do not get that one, then I will have none.”
sentences.i: Then the second answered from the other side of the hill, and pointed at the man who walked at the king’s right hand: “Helo! Helo! If I do not get that one, then I will have none at all.”
sentences.n: antworde = antwortete; zweide = zweite (the tale also spells it tweide); Side = Seite. “rechter Hand” is an old adverbial phrase, at the right hand, on the right.

sentences.t: Da reip de jüngeste, un weis up den, de linker Hand gink, „helo! helo! wenn ik den nig kriege, so will ik keinen.“
sentences.l: Then the youngest called, and pointed at the one who went at the left hand, “helo! helo! if I do not get that one, then I will have none.”
sentences.i: Then the youngest called out, and pointed at the man who walked on the left: “Helo! Helo! If I do not get that one, then I will have none at all.”
sentences.n: jüngeste = jüngste. The three cries are word for word the same, which is how these tales mark a set of three; only the man pointed at changes.

sentences.t: Dat wören averst de beden Ministers.
sentences.l: Those, however, were the two ministers.
sentences.n: averst = aber; beden = beiden, the two. The men flanking the king are his ministers, so between them the three girls have chosen the king and his two great officers.

sentences.t: Dat hörde de Künig alles, un ase von der Jagd heime kummen was, leit he de drei Mäkens to sik kummen un fragete se wat se da gistern am Berge segd hedden.
sentences.l: The king heard all that, and when he had come home from the hunt, he let the three girls come to him and asked them what they had said there yesterday on the hill.
sentences.i: The king heard every word of it; and when he had come home from the hunt he had the three girls brought to him, and asked what it was they had said the day before on the hill.
sentences.n: hörde = hörte; heime = heim; leit = ließ; fragete = fragte; gistern = gestern; hedden = hätten. “leit he … kummen” is lassen with an infinitive, to have someone come. hedden is the subjunctive of reported speech, marking the words as theirs and not the narrator’s.

sentences.t: Dat wullen se nig seggen, de Künig frog awerst de ölleste, ob se ün wol tom Manne hewen wulle?
sentences.l: That they would not say, but the king asked the eldest whether she would have him for a husband?
sentences.i: They would not say it; but the king asked the eldest whether she would have him for her husband.
sentences.n: wullen = wollten; frog = fragte; ölleste = älteste; ün = ihn; wulle = wollte. hewen here is haben, to have — “tom Manne hewen” = zum Manne haben, to take as husband. The question mark stands although the question is only reported.

sentences.t: Da segde se ja, un ere beiden Süstern friggeten de beiden Ministers, denn se wören alle drei scheun un schir (klar, schön) von Angesicht, besunners de Künigin, de hadde Hare ase Flass.
sentences.l: Then she said yes, and her two sisters married the two ministers, for they were all three fair and bright (klar, schön) of countenance, especially the queen: she had hair like flax.
sentences.i: Then she said yes, and her two sisters married the two ministers; for all three were fair and clear of face, and the queen most of all — she had hair like flax.
sentences.n: segde = sagte; friggeten = freiten, married (friggen = freien); scheun = schön; besunners = besonders; Hare = Haare; Flass = Flachs. schir (schier) is glossed by the Grimms themselves as klar, schön. Flax is pale gold, so hers is the fairest hair of the three. “Da segde se ja” has ja in its plain sense, yes; inside a sentence, later in the tale, the same word is only a particle.

sentences.t: De beiden Süstern awerst kregen keine Kinner, un ase de Künig mal verreisen moste, let he se tor Künigin kummen, um se up to munnern, denn se was grae (gerad) swanger.
sentences.l: The two sisters, however, got no children, and when the king once had to travel away, he let them come to the queen, in order to cheer her up, for she was just (gerad) with child.
sentences.i: But the two sisters got no children; and when the king once had to go away on a journey, he had them come to the queen to cheer her, for she was just then with child.
sentences.n: kregen = kriegten, got; moste = mußte; let = ließ; tor = zur; swanger = schwanger; was here is war, was — a Low German form that looks like the High German question-word. grae is glossed by the Grimms as gerad, just then. “up to munnern” = aufzumuntern, to cheer up, a separable verb with the zu of the infinitive standing between particle and stem.

sentences.t: Se kreg en kleinen Jungen, de hadde ’n ritsch roen (rothen) Stern mit up de Weld.
sentences.l: She got a little boy, who had brought a bright red (rothen) star with him onto the world.
sentences.i: She bore a little boy, who brought a bright red star into the world with him.
sentences.n: kreg = kriegte, got, bore; Weld = Welt. roen is glossed by the Grimms as rothen (modern roten), red. ritsch is an intensifying word here, something like “vivid, glowing.” “mit up de Weld” = mit auf die Welt: he brought the mark with him at birth, and it is what will name him at the end.

sentences.t: Da sehden de beiden Süstern, eine tor annern, se wullen den hübsken Jungen in’t Water werpen.
sentences.l: Then the two sisters said, the one to the other, they would throw the pretty boy into the water.
sentences.i: Then the two sisters said to one another that they would throw the pretty boy into the water.
sentences.n: sehden = sagten; hübsken = hübschen; werpen = werfen. The clipped in’t is in dat, into the — here the ’t is the article, not the pronoun “it.”

sentences.t: Wie se’n darin worpen hadden (ick glöwe, et is de Weser west), da flügt ’n Vügelken in de Högte, dat sank
sentences.l: When they had thrown him in (I believe it was the Weser), then a little bird flies up into the height, which sang
sentences.i: When they had thrown him in — I believe it was the Weser — a little bird flew up into the air, and it sang:
sentences.n: se’n = se ün, they … him; worpen = geworfen; Högte = Höhe; sank here is sang, not sank. This round bracket is not a gloss but the teller’s own aside, printed as the Grimms heard it: ick glöwe = ich glaube, west = gewesen. The Weser is the great river of this country, which sets the tale where it was told. Note too the slide into the present tense, flügt (fliegt), at the moment the bird rises.

sentences.t:
„tom Daude bereit,
up wietern Bescheid
tom Lilienstrus:
wacker Junge, bist du’s?“
sentences.l:
“ready for death,
upon further word
to the lily-bouquet:
fine boy, is it you?”
sentences.i:
“Ready for the grave,
awaiting further word,
bound for the lilies:
brave boy, is it you?”
sentences.n: The bird’s song, and the darkest four lines in the tale — sung over a drowned child. tom Daude = zum Tode; wietern = weiteren; Bescheid is word, answer, ruling, so “up wietern Bescheid” is until further word; Lilienstrus = Lilienstrauß, a bunch of lilies, the flowers of a grave; wacker is brave, fine, sturdy; du’s = du es. The lines are cryptic in the German as well, and no reading of them is certain; they work as a charm rather than as a sentence.

sentences.t: Da dat de beiden hörten, kregen se de Angst up’n Lieve un makten, dat se fort keimen.
sentences.l: When the two heard that, they got the fear upon their body and made that they got away.
sentences.i: When the two heard that, terror came over them, and they made off as fast as they could.
sentences.n: Lieve = Leibe; makten = machten; keimen = kämen; fort = fort, away. “de Angst up’n Lieve kriegen” is to get the fear on one’s body, that is, to be seized with terror. “maken, dat …” is to see to it that one does a thing.

sentences.t: Wie de Künig na Hus kam, sehden se to üm de Künigin hedde ’n Hund kregen.
sentences.l: When the king came home, they said to him the queen had got a dog.
sentences.i: When the king came home, they told him the queen had given birth to a dog.
sentences.n: na Hus = nach Haus; üm = ihm; hedde = hätte; kregen = gekriegt. The subjunctive hedde marks this as their lie and not the narrator’s report. To say that a woman has borne an animal is the old accusation that costs her everything.

sentences.t: Da segde de Künig „wat Gott deiet, dat is wole dahn.“
sentences.l: Then the king said, “what God does, that is well done.”
sentences.n: deiet = tut; wole = wohl; dahn = getan. “Wat Gott deit, dat is wol dahn” is a proverb and the opening of a well-known hymn; the king answers his own grief with a formula, and he will say it again, a little shorter, over the second child.

sentences.t: Et wunde averst ’n Fisker an den Water, de fiskede den kleinen Jungen wier herut, ase noch ewen lebennig was, un da sine Fru kene Kinner hadde, foerden (fütterten) s’en up.
sentences.l: But there dwelt a fisherman on the water, who fished the little boy out again, as [he] was still just alive, and since his wife had no children, they fed (fütterten) him up.
sentences.i: But there lived a fisherman by the water, and he fished the little boy out again, just barely alive; and since his wife had no children, they brought him up.
sentences.n: wunde here is wohnte, dwelt — not die Wunde, a wound. fiskede = fischte; wier = wieder; herut = heraus; ewen = eben, just; lebennig = lebendig; kene = keine; s’en = se ün, they him. foerden is glossed by the Grimms as fütterten: “upfoeren” is to feed up, to rear. The subject is left out again — “ase noch ewen lebennig was” — so the English supplies [he]; that bracket is ours.

sentences.t: Na’n Jaar was de Künig wier verreist, da krig de Künigin wier ’n Jungen, den namen de beiden falsken Süstern un warpen ’n auck in’t Water, da flügt dat Vügelken wier in de Högte un sank:
sentences.l: After a year the king had travelled away again, then the queen got another boy, whom the two false sisters took and threw him too into the water; then the little bird flies up into the height again and sang:
sentences.i: A year later the king had gone away again, and the queen bore another boy; the two false sisters took him and threw him too into the water, and again the little bird rose into the air and sang:
sentences.n: Na’n Jaar = nach einem Jahr; krig = kriegte; namen here is nahmen, took, and not der Name; warpen = warfen; falsken = falschen. The tale repeats itself almost word for word — that is how it counts its three children.

sentences.t:
„tom Daude bereit,
up wietern Bescheid
tom Lilienstrus:
wacker Junge, bist du’s?“
sentences.l:
“ready for death,
upon further word
to the lily-bouquet:
fine boy, is it you?”
sentences.i:
“Ready for the grave,
awaiting further word,
bound for the lilies:
brave boy, is it you?”
sentences.n: The same song again, unchanged, over the second child.

sentences.t: Un wie de Künig torügge kam, sehden se to üm, de Künigin hedde wier ’n Hund bekummen, un he segde wier „wat Gott deit, dat is wole dahn.“
sentences.l: And when the king came back, they said to him the queen had got another dog, and he said again, “what God does, that is well done.”
sentences.i: And when the king came back, they told him the queen had borne another dog; and again he said: “What God does, that is well done.”
sentences.n: torügge = zurück; bekummen = bekommen; deit = tut, the shorter form of deiet in the first saying. The proverb comes back unchanged — it is all the answer he has.

sentences.t: Awerst de Fisker trok düsen auck ut den Water un foerd ’n up.
sentences.l: But the fisherman drew this one too out of the water and fed him up.
sentences.i: But the fisherman drew this one too out of the water and reared him.
sentences.n: trok = zog; düsen = diesen; ut = aus; foerd = fütterte, the same “upfoeren” as before.

sentences.t: Da verreisede de Künig wier, un de Künigin kreg ’n klein Mäken, dat warpen de falsken Süstern auck in’t Water.
sentences.l: Then the king travelled away again, and the queen got a little girl, whom the false sisters threw too into the water.
sentences.i: Then the king went away again, and the queen bore a little girl, and the false sisters threw her too into the water.
sentences.n: verreisede = verreiste; Mäken = Mädchen. Because Mäken is neuter, the relative that picks it up is dat, das — grammar and not disrespect; High German does the same with Mädchen.

sentences.t: Da flügt dat Vügelken wier in de Högte un sank
sentences.l: Then the little bird flies up into the height again and sang
sentences.i: Then the little bird rose into the air again, and sang
sentences.n: The same line as before, and the same slide into the present at the moment of rising: flügt = fliegt, sank = sang.

sentences.t:
„tom Daude bereit,
up wietern Bescheid
sentences.l:
“ready for death,
upon further word
sentences.i:
“Ready for the grave,
awaiting further word,
sentences.n: The 1857 text prints this third singing as two blocks with nothing between them, and this edition keeps them as it found them. The first two lines are unchanged from the earlier singings.

sentences.t:
tom Lilienstrus:
wacker Mäken, bist du’s?“
sentences.l:
to the lily-bouquet:
fine girl, is it you?”
sentences.i:
bound for the lilies:
brave girl, is it you?”
sentences.n: One word only has changed in the whole song: Junge has become Mäken, the boy a girl.

sentences.t: Un wie de Künig na Hus kam, sehden se to üm, de Künigin hedde ’ne Katte kregt.
sentences.l: And when the king came home, they said to him the queen had got a cat.
sentences.i: And when the king came home, they told him the queen had borne a cat.
sentences.n: Katte = Katze; kregt = gekriegt. Dog, dog, cat: the third lie is the one that breaks him.

sentences.t: Da worde de Künig beuse, un leit sine Fru in’t Gefängnis smieten, da hed se lange Jaare in setten.
sentences.l: Then the king became angry, and had his wife thrown into the prison; there she sat long years in it.
sentences.i: Then the king grew angry, and had his wife thrown into prison, and there she sat for long years.
sentences.n: worde = wurde; beuse = böse; smieten = schmeißen, to fling; hed = hat; setten = gesessen. “da hed se … in setten” = da hat sie darin gesessen; the in belongs with the da, as English says “in there.”

sentences.t: De Kinner wören unnerdes anewassen, da gink de ölleste mal mit annern Jungens herut to fisken, da wüllt ün de annern Jungens nig twisken sik hewen un segget „du Fündling, gaa du diner Wege.“
sentences.l: The children had grown up meanwhile; then the eldest once went out with other lads to fish, and the other lads will not have him among them and say, “you foundling, go your ways.”
sentences.i: Meanwhile the children had grown up; and once the eldest went out fishing with other lads, and the other lads would not have him among them, and said: “You foundling, be off on your way.”
sentences.n: unnerdes = unterdes; anewassen = angewachsen, grown up; wüllt = wollen; twisken = zwischen; hewen = haben; segget = sagen; gaa = geh; diner Wege = deiner Wege. “seiner Wege gehen” is the set phrase for going off about one’s own business. The telling slips into the present again at the moment of the insult.

sentences.t: Da ward he gans bedröwet un fräggt den olen Fisker ob dat war wöre?
sentences.l: Then he became quite sad and asks the old fisherman whether that was true?
sentences.i: Then he grew quite downcast, and asked the old fisherman whether it was true.
sentences.n: gans = ganz; bedröwet = betrübt; fräggt = fragt; wöre = wäre. war here is wahr, true — not the past of sein that the same three letters carry elsewhere.

sentences.t: De vertellt ün dat he mal fisked hedde, un hedde ün ut den Water troken (gezogen).
sentences.l: He tells him that he had once been fishing, and had drawn (gezogen) him out of the water.
sentences.i: He told him that he had once been out fishing, and had drawn him out of the water.
sentences.n: vertellt = erzählt; fisked = gefischt; troken is glossed by the Grimms as gezogen. De at the head of the sentence is a demonstrative, that one — the fisherman.

sentences.t: Da segd he he wulle furt un sinen Teiten (Vater) söken.
sentences.l: Then he says he would go away and seek his father (Vater).
sentences.i: Then he said he would go away and look for his father.
sentences.n: segd = sagt; wulle = wollte; furt = fort; söken = suchen. Teiten is glossed by the Grimms as Vater — a nursery word for father, like our “dad.” The verb of motion is left out after the modal: he wulle furt, he would [go] away.

sentences.t: De Fisker de biddet ’n he mögde doch bliven, awerst he let sik gar nicht hallen, bis de Fisker et tolest to givt.
sentences.l: The fisherman, he begs him he might yet stay, but he let himself not be held at all, until the fisherman at last gives in.
sentences.i: The fisherman begged him to stay after all, but he would not be held back at all, until at last the fisherman gave in.
sentences.n: biddet = bittet; mögde = möchte; bliven = bleiben; hallen = halten; tolest = zuletzt; “to givt” = gibt zu, gives in, with the particle standing first. “De Fisker de biddet” takes the subject up again with a pronoun — the fisherman, he begs — which is ordinary Low German and gives the sentence its spoken swing.

sentences.t: Da givt he sik up den Weg un geit meere Dage hinner’n anner, endlich kümmt he vor ’n graut allmächtig Water, davor steit ’ne ole Fru un fiskede.
sentences.l: Then he gives himself upon the way and goes several days one after another; at last he comes before a great, mighty water, and before it stands an old woman and was fishing.
sentences.i: So he set out on his way and went for several days one after another, until at last he came to a great and mighty water; and before it stood an old woman, fishing.
sentences.n: “sik up den Weg gieven” = sich auf den Weg geben, to set out. meere = mehrere, several; hinner’n anner = hintereinander, one after another; graut = groß; steit = steht; ole = alte. The tale keeps sliding between present and past — givt, geit, kümmt, then fiskede — as a told story does, and the translations follow it.

sentences.t: „Guden Dag, Moer,“ segde de Junge. „Groten Dank.“
sentences.l: “Good day, mother,” said the boy. “Great thanks.”
sentences.i: “Good day, mother,” said the boy. “Many thanks.”
sentences.n: Guden Dag = guten Tag; Moer = Mutter, the ordinary respectful address to an old woman, as our “mother” once was. “Groten Dank” = großen Dank is her whole answer to the greeting.

sentences.t: „Du süst da wol lange fisken, e du ’n Fisk fängest.“
sentences.l: “You will be fishing there a long while, before you catch a fish.”
sentences.n: e here is ehe, before. fängest = fängst. süst is the harder word: it stands for a form of sollen or werden, so the line runs “you are like to fish a long while yet”; the exact form is not certainly explained. The boy is pert to a stranger, and that is the first test.

sentences.t: „Un du wol lange söken, e du dinen Teiten findst. Wie wust du der denn da över’t Water kummen?“ sehde de Fru.
sentences.l: “And you a long while seeking, before you find your father. How do you mean to get over the water there?” said the woman.
sentences.i: “And you will be seeking a long while before you find your father. How do you mean to get over the water there?” said the woman.
sentences.n: The old woman answers him in his own words, leaving out the verb just as he did — “un du wol lange söken.” dinen = deinen; findst = findest; wust = willst; över’t = över dat, over the. der in this line is a small filler word of the dialect and carries no weight of its own.

sentences.t: „Ja, dat mag Gott witten.“
sentences.l: “Yes, God may know that.”
sentences.i: “Yes, God alone may know that.”
sentences.n: witten here is wissen, to know — not the colour word it resembles. “dat mag Gott witten” is a shrug: heaven knows. It is also what settles the meeting, for he never asks her for anything.

sentences.t: Da nümmt de ole Fru ün up den Rüggen un dragt ’n derdörch, un he söcht lange Tiid un kann sinen Teiten nig finnen.
sentences.l: Then the old woman takes him upon her back and carries him through, and he seeks a long time and cannot find his father.
sentences.i: Then the old woman took him on her back and carried him across, and he sought a long time and could not find his father.
sentences.n: nümmt = nimmt; Rüggen = Rücken; dragt = trägt; derdörch = dadurch, through it; söcht = sucht; Tiid = Zeit; finnen = finden. She carries him over unasked — and it does him no good at all, which is the point of the three journeys.

sentences.t: Ase nu wol ’n Jahr veröwer is, da trekt de tweide auck ut un will sinen Broer söken.
sentences.l: When now fully a year is over, then the second sets out too and will seek his brother.
sentences.i: When a full year was over, the second set out as well, to look for his brother.
sentences.n: veröwer = vorüber; trekt … ut = zieht aus, sets out, a separable verb; tweide = zweite; Broer = Bruder.

sentences.t: He kümmt an dat Water, un da geit et ün ewen so, ase sinen Broer.
sentences.l: He comes to the water, and there it goes with him just as with his brother.
sentences.i: He came to the water, and there it went with him just as it had with his brother.
sentences.n: “et geit ün ewen so” = es geht ihm eben so, it fares with him just the same. ase = wie, as.

sentences.t: Nu was nur noch de Dochter allein to Hus, de jammerde so viel na eren Broern, dat se upt lest auck den Fisker bad he mögte se treken laten, se wulle ere Broerkes söken.
sentences.l: Now only the daughter was still alone at home, and she grieved so much after her brothers that at the last she too begged the fisherman he might let her go, she would seek her little brothers.
sentences.i: Now only the daughter was left at home, and she grieved so for her brothers that at last she too begged the fisherman to let her go, for she would look for her little brothers.
sentences.n: jammerde = jammerte, lamented; na = nach; eren = ihren; upt lest = aufs letzt, at last; bad here is bat, begged, from bidden — not das Bad, a bath; mögte = möchte; treken = ziehen, to travel, to go; Broerkes = Brüderchen, with the Low German diminutive -ke.

sentences.t: Da kam se auck bie den grauten Water, da sehde se tor olen Fru „guden Dag, Moer.“ „Groten Dank.“
sentences.l: Then she too came to the great water, and there she said to the old woman, “good day, mother.” “Great thanks.”
sentences.i: Then she too came to the great water, and said to the old woman: “Good day, mother.” “Many thanks.”
sentences.n: The greeting is word for word her brothers’, and so is the answer; the difference is in the line she adds next. bie = bei.

sentences.t: „Gott helpe ju bie juen fisken.“
sentences.l: “God help you at your fishing.”
sentences.n: helpe = helfe; ju = euch; juen = euren. This is the old greeting spoken to anyone at work, and it is the hinge of the whole tale: the girl blesses the old woman’s labour, and her brothers did not.

sentences.t: Ase de ole Fru dat hörde, da word se ganz fründlich un drog se över’t Water un gab er ’n Roe (Ruthe),
sentences.l: When the old woman heard that, she became quite friendly and carried her over the water and gave her a rod (Ruthe),
sentences.i: When the old woman heard that, she grew quite kindly, and carried her over the water and gave her a rod,
sentences.n: word = wurde; fründlich = freundlich; drog = trug; er here is ihr, to her, not er, he. Roe is glossed by the Grimms as Ruthe (modern Rute), a rod or switch.

sentences.t: un sehde to er „nu gah man jümmer up düsen Wege to, mine Dochter, un wenn du bie einen groten swarten Hund vorbei kümmst, so must du still un drist un one to lachen un one ün an to kicken, vorbie gaan.
sentences.l: and said to her, “now just keep going on along this way, my daughter, and when you come past a great black dog, then you must, quietly and boldly and without laughing and without looking at him, go past.
sentences.i: and said to her: “Now just keep on along this road, my daughter; and when you come past a great black dog, you must go by quietly and boldly, without laughing and without looking at him.
sentences.n: man here is nur, just, only — a small word doing a great deal of work in Low German. jümmer = immer; mine = meine; groten = großen; must = mußt; drist = dreist, bold; one = ohne; kicken = gucken, to look; gaan = gehen. The whole instruction is one long conditional, and its verb, vorbie gaan, waits to the very end.

sentences.t: Dann kümmest du an ’n grot open Schlot, up’n Süll (Schwelle) most du de Roe fallen laten un stracks dörch dat Schlott an den annern Side wier herut gahen;
sentences.l: Then you come to a great open castle; on the threshold (Schwelle) you must let the rod fall and go straight through the castle and out again at the other side;
sentences.i: Then you will come to a great open castle; on the threshold you must let the rod fall, and go straight through the castle and out again on the other side;
sentences.n: kümmest = kommst; grot = groß; open = offen (not the English word it looks like); Schlot and Schlott are both Schloß, the castle; most = mußt; stracks = straightway; dörch = durch; gahen = gehen. Süll is glossed by the Grimms as Schwelle, the threshold — and the rod left lying on it is what will let her out again.

sentences.t: da is ’n olen Brunnen, darut is ’n groten Boom wassen, daran hänget ’n Vugel im Buer, den nümm af:
sentences.l: there is an old well, out of it a great tree has grown, on it hangs a bird in a cage; take that down:
sentences.i: there is an old well, and out of it a great tree has grown, and on the tree hangs a bird in a cage; take it down:
sentences.n: darut = daraus; Boom = Baum; wassen = gewachsen; hänget = hängt; “nümm af” = nimm ab, take down. Buer here is the cage — Low German Buer, High German Bauer in its old sense of a birdcage, and nothing to do with a farmer.

sentences.t: dann nümm noch ’n Glas Water ut den Brunnen un gaa mit düsen beiden den sülvigen Weg wier torügge:
sentences.l: then take also a glass of water out of the well and go with these two the same way back again:
sentences.i: then take a glass of water from the well as well, and go back the same way with the two of them:
sentences.n: sülvigen = selbigen, the selfsame. The bird and the glass of water are the two things the tale has been keeping back for its ending.

sentences.t: up den Süll nümm de Roe auck wier mit, un wenn du dann wier bie den Hund vorbie kummst, so schlah ün in’t Gesicht, awerst sü to dat du ün treppest, un dann kumm nur wier to me torügge.“
sentences.l: on the threshold take the rod with you again too, and when you then come past the dog again, then strike him in the face, but see to it that you hit him, and then just come back to me again.”
sentences.i: take the rod with you again from the threshold; and when you come past the dog once more, strike him in the face — but see that you hit him — and then come back to me.”
sentences.n: schlah = schlag; “sü to” = sieh zu, see to it; treppest = triffst; me = mi, mir, to me. The blow is not cruelty: it is the stroke that breaks an enchantment, and it has to land.

sentences.t: Da fand se et grade so, ase de Fru et sagd hadde, un up den Rückwege da fand se de beiden Broer, de sik de halve Welt durchsöcht hadden.
sentences.l: Then she found it just so, as the woman had said it, and on the way back she found the two brothers, who had searched half the world through.
sentences.i: And she found it just as the woman had said; and on the way back she found her two brothers, who had searched half the world through.
sentences.n: grade = gerade; sagd = gesagt; halve = halbe; durchsöcht = durchsucht. “sik … durchsöken” takes the accusative of what is searched: they had searched their way through half the world.

sentences.t: Se gienk tosammen bis wo de swarte Hund an den Weg lag, den schlog se in’t Gesicht, da word et ’n schönen Prinz, de geit mit ünen, bis an dat Water.
sentences.l: They went together to where the black dog lay by the way; she struck it in the face, and then it became a handsome prince, who goes with them, as far as the water.
sentences.i: They went on together to where the black dog lay by the road; she struck it in the face, and at once it became a handsome prince, who went with them as far as the water.
sentences.n: gienk here is plural, they went — the dialect does not always mark the ending. schlog = schlug; word = wurde; ünen = ihnen. The dog is the enchanted prince, and the blow the girl was told to strike is what frees him.

sentences.t: Da stand da noch de ole Fru, de frögede sik ser, da se alle wier da wören, un drog se alle över’t Water, un dann gink se auck weg, denn se was nu erlöst.
sentences.l: There the old woman was still standing, who rejoiced greatly that they were all there again, and carried them all over the water, and then she too went away, for she was now released.
sentences.i: The old woman was still standing there, and she rejoiced greatly that they were all back again, and carried them all over the water; and then she too went away, for she was released now.
sentences.n: frögede sik = freute sich; ser = sehr; drog = trug. Nothing has told us that the old woman was under a spell as well; the tale says it here, in passing, and lets her go.

sentences.t: De annern awerst gingen alle na den olen Fisker, un alle wören froh dat se sik wier funnen hadden, den Vügel awerst hüngen se an der Wand.
sentences.l: But the others all went to the old fisherman, and all were glad that they had found each other again; the bird, however, they hung on the wall.
sentences.i: But the others all went to the old fisherman, and all were glad to have found one another again; and the bird they hung on the wall.
sentences.n: funnen = gefunden; Vügel = Vogel; hüngen = hingen. The bird is hung on the wall without a word of explanation — and it is the bird that will speak at the end.

sentences.t: De tweide Suhn kunne awerst nig to Huse rasten, un nam ’n Flitzebogen un gink up de Jagd.
sentences.l: The second son, however, could not rest at home, and took a bow and went to the hunt.
sentences.i: But the second son could not rest at home; he took a bow and went out hunting.
sentences.n: Suhn = Sohn; kunne = konnte; nam = nahm; Flitzebogen = Flitzbogen, a light hand-bow. He goes hunting as the king does, and the tale is bringing father and son into the same wood.

sentences.t: Wie he möe was, nam he sine Flötepipen un mackte ’n Stücksken.
sentences.l: When he was tired, he took his pipe and made a little piece.
sentences.i: When he grew tired, he took out his pipe and played a little tune.
sentences.n: möe = müde; Flötepipen = Flötenpfeife, a flute or whistle; mackte = machte; Stücksken = Stückchen, a little piece of music, with the Low German diminutive -sken.

sentences.t: De Künig awerst wör auck up de Jagd un hörde dat, da gieng he hin, un wie he den Jungen drap, so sehde he „we hett die verlöwt hier to jagen?“
sentences.l: But the king was at the hunt too and heard it, so he went over there, and when he met the boy, he said, “who has allowed you to hunt here?”
sentences.i: But the king was out hunting too and heard it, and he went over; and when he met the boy he said: “Who gave you leave to hunt here?”
sentences.n: wör = war; drap = traf, met; we = wer, who — not the English word it resembles; hett = hat; verlöwt = erlaubt. die here is dir, to you, and not the article it looks like.

sentences.t: „O, neimes (niemand).“ „Wen hörst du dann to?“
sentences.l: “Oh, nobody (niemand).” “To whom do you belong then?”
sentences.i: “Oh, nobody.” “Whom do you belong to, then?”
sentences.n: neimes is glossed by the Grimms as niemand. “to hören” is zugehören, to belong to — the to stands at the end of the question and belongs with hörst, so this is not about hearing at all. Wen stands where High German would have wem.

sentences.t: „Ik bin den Fisker sin Suhn.“ „De hett ja keine Kinner.“
sentences.l: “I am the fisherman his son.” “But he has no children.”
sentences.i: “I am the fisherman’s son.” “But he has no children.”
sentences.n: “den Fisker sin Suhn” is the ordinary Low German possessive — the fisherman, his son — where High German uses the genitive, des Fischers Sohn. ja here is not yes but the particle appealing to what is known: but he has none.

sentences.t: „Wenn du’t nig glöwen wust, so kum mit.“
sentences.l: “If you will not believe it, then come along.”
sentences.n: du’t = du et, you it; glöwen = glauben; wust = willst; kum = komm. The boy answers a king without any ceremony, and the tale lets him.

sentences.t: Dat dehe de Künig un frog den Fisker, de vertälle ün alles, un dat Vügelken an der Wand fing an to singen
sentences.l: That the king did, and asked the fisherman, who told him everything, and the little bird on the wall began to sing
sentences.i: The king did so, and asked the fisherman, who told him everything; and the little bird on the wall began to sing:
sentences.n: dehe = tat; vertälle = erzählte. “fing an to singen” is anfangen with an infinitive, and in Low German the to (High German zu) stands just where English puts its “to.”

sentences.t:
„de Möhme (Mutter) sitt allein,
wol in dat Kerkerlein.
o Künig, edeles Blod,
dat sind dine Kinner god.
De falsken Süstern beide
de dehen de Kinnerkes Leide,
wol in des Waters Grund,
wo se de Fisker fund.“
sentences.l:
“the mother (Mutter) sits alone,
indeed, in the little prison.
o king, noble blood,
those are your children, good ones.
The two false sisters,
they did the little children harm,
indeed in the water’s ground,
where the fisherman found them.”
sentences.i:
“The mother sits alone,
there in the little prison cell.
O king, of noble blood,
these are your children, and good ones.
The two false sisters,
they did the little children harm,
down in the depths of the water,
where the fisherman found them.”
sentences.n: The bird’s second song tells the whole story in eight lines. Möhme is glossed by the Grimms themselves as Mutter; the word usually means an aunt or kinswoman, and their bracket settles which is meant. sitt = sitzt; wol = wohl, here filling out the line, and the literal renders it the same way in both places it stands; Kerkerlein is the diminutive of Kerker, a prison; edeles Blod = edles Blut; dine = deine; god = gut; dehen = taten; Kinnerkes = Kinderchen; “Leide dohn” = Leid tun, to do harm; Waters = Wassers; fund = fand. The verse rhymes in pairs, and the word order is bent to the rhyme, which is why god stands after its noun.

sentences.t: Da erschraken se alle, un de Künig nahm den Vugel, den Fisker un de drei Kinner mit sik na den Schlotte un leit dat Gefänknis upschluten un nam sine Fru wier herut, de was awerst gans kränksch un elennig woren.
sentences.l: Then they were all startled, and the king took the bird, the fisherman and the three children with him to the castle and had the prison unlocked and took his wife out again; but she had become quite sickly and wretched.
sentences.i: Then they were all struck with horror, and the king took the bird, the fisherman and the three children with him to the castle, and had the prison unlocked and brought his wife out again; but she had grown quite sickly and wretched.
sentences.n: Vugel = Vogel; Gefänknis = Gefängnis; upschluten = aufschließen, to unlock; kränksch = kränklich; elennig = elend; woren = geworden. The long years in the cell have done what the sisters wanted, and the tale does not soften it.

sentences.t: Da gav er de Dochter von den Water ut den Brunnen to drinken, da war se frisk un gesund.
sentences.l: Then the daughter gave her of the water out of the well to drink, and she was fresh and well.
sentences.i: Then the daughter gave her the water from the well to drink, and she grew fresh and well again.
sentences.n: gav = gab; er here is ihr, to her, as it was when the old woman gave her the rod; war is the plain past, was — where the tale means became it writes ward, as it does when the boy grows downcast — and the change follows from the drinking; frisk = frisch. This is what the glass of water was carried back for.

sentences.t: De beiden falsken Süstern wören awerst verbrennt, un de Dochter friggede den Prinzen.
sentences.l: The two false sisters, however, were burnt, and the daughter married the prince.
sentences.i: But the two false sisters were burnt, and the daughter married the prince.
sentences.n: verbrennt = verbrannt; friggede = freite, married. Burning was the punishment for witchcraft and for the killing of children; the tale states it in half a line and ends.

glossary.bad: bad — bat (bidden, bitten), begged (3rd sg. preterite; not das Bad, a bath)
glossary.beden: beden — beiden, the two, both (LG beden = beiden; not gebeten)
glossary.berge: berge — der Berg, mountain (dat. sg. with old -e: unner den Berge, am Berge)
glossary.der: der — der / die, the; in ‘wie wust du der denn …’ an unstressed filler word of the dialect
glossary.die: die — di, dir, to you (dative of du; not the article)
glossary.e: e — ehe, before (conjunction; LG e = ehe)
glossary.en: en — ein / einen, a, one; in s’en, se’n it is ün, ihn, him (clitic)
glossary.er: er — ihr, to her (dative of se; LG er = ihr, not er, he)
glossary.gans: gans — ganz, quite, entirely (LG gans = ganz; not die Gans, goose)
glossary.gerad: gerad — gerade, just, just then (the Grimms’ gloss of grae; temporal, not ‘straight’)
glossary.hen: hen — hin, gone by, ago (temporal: dusent Jaare hen; not directional ‘thither’)
glossary.hewen: hewen — hebben, haben, to have (LG hewen = haben; not Himmel)
glossary.hörst: hörst — hören … to (zugehören), belong to (2nd sg.; wen hörst du to = wem gehörst du zu)
glossary.ja: ja — ja, yes (Da segde se ja; „Ja, dat mag Gott witten“); elsewhere the particle, after all
glossary.junge: junge — der Junge, boy, lad (noun; not the adjective jung)
glossary.jungen: jungen — der Junge, boy (acc./dat. sg. of the noun)
glossary.kregen: kregen — kriegen, got (3rd pl. preterite); also gekriegt, got (past part.: hedde ’n Hund kregen)
glossary.mal: mal — mal, einmal, once, one day (adverb; not das Mal, the noun)
glossary.man: man — nur, just, only (LG particle; not the impersonal pronoun man)
glossary.meere: meere — mehr, mehrere, more, several (LG; not das Meer, the sea)
glossary.n: ’n — ein / einen, a, one; also ün, ihn, him (biddet ’n) and den (up’n Süll = up den Süll)
glossary.namen: namen — nahmen (nehmen), took (3rd pl. preterite; not der Name)
glossary.rechter: rechter — recht, right (rechter Hand = at the right hand, old adverbial phrase)
glossary.ritsch: ritsch — ritsch, vivid, glowing (intensifier before a colour; not the snip-snap sound word)
glossary.s: ’s — es, it (bist du’s); also se, sie, they (s’en = se ün, they him)
glossary.san: san — san, so, ever so (intensifier with geren, gladly; the form is not certainly explained)
glossary.sank: sank — sang (singen), sang (3rd sg. preterite; LG sank = sang, not sinken)
glossary.segd: segd — seggen, sagen, says (3rd sg.); also gesagt, said (past part.: segd hedden)
glossary.sei: sei — se, sie, they (subject pronoun; not the imperative of sein)
glossary.seien: seien — sehen, saw (3rd pl. preterite, LG seien = sahen; not a form of sein)
glossary.t: ’t — dat, the (article after a preposition: in’t = in dat, över’t = över dat); also et, it (du’t)
glossary.verbrennt: verbrennt — verbrannt (verbrennen), burnt (past participle: wören verbrennt, were burnt)
glossary.war: war — wahr, true (ob dat war wöre); elsewhere war (sein), was
glossary.was: was — war (sein), was (3rd sg. preterite; the question-word here is wat)
glossary.weg: weg — der Weg, way, road (noun: up den Weg, an den Weg); also weg, away (gink se weg)
glossary.wege: wege — der Weg, way (dat. sg.: up düsen Wege to; old genitive in diner Wege)
glossary.weis: weis — wies (weisen), pointed (3rd sg. preterite; weis up = wies auf, pointed at)
glossary.wen: wen — wem, to whom (dative; wen hörst du to = wem gehörst du zu)
glossary.witten: witten — wissen, to know (LG witten = wissen; not witt, white)
glossary.wunde: wunde — wohnte (wohnen), dwelt (3rd sg. preterite; not die Wunde, a wound)
